title: Mercy to captives
hook: the prisoners of Badr are fed well, and some freed for teaching Muslim children to read

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wells of Badr, three hundred against a thousand. Your line was few against many. Did you take one step on something that felt too big? Day two hundred sixty-five.

The battle is over. And now the Muslims of Medina have something they've never had before: about seventy prisoners. These are men from Mecca, some of whom had mocked them, boycotted them, driven them from their homes. Some are relatives: cousins, brothers, an uncle. In that world, what happened to captives was often brutal. So picture the scene: the prisoners are marched back to Medina, tied up, and divided among Muslim households to be held until their families can pay a ransom. What would you expect? What happened next is one of the stories Muslims tell most proudly about their early history. Today: mercy to captives.
screen: `SEVENTY PRISONERS.` → `THE MEN WHO DROVE THEM OUT.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU EXPECT?`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions to treat the captives well. And the early biographer Ibn Ishaq keeps the memory of one prisoner, Abu 'Aziz, who described it afterward. He said the family of Ansar holding him would give him the bread, which was the better food, and eat only dates themselves, because of what the Prophet had told them. He said he'd hand the bread back, embarrassed, and they'd give it right back to him. Food was not plentiful in Medina. They gave the enemy the good part. The Qur'an praises this kind of thing in a later surah: the righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, for the love of God, wanting no reward and no thanks. Then there was the ransom. Families in Mecca paid to free their men. But some prisoners were poor, and had no one to pay. And a report from Ibn 'Abbas, in the Musnad of Ahmad, says the Prophet set a different price for some of them: teach ten children of the Ansar to read and write, and you're free. Think about what that says. A young community, fighting for its life, and what it asks of its enemies is literacy for its kids. Tradition says one of the children who learned to write this way was Zayd ibn Thabit, who would later become one of the main scribes of the Qur'an. And one more detail: the Prophet's own uncle, al-'Abbas, was among the captives. The sources say the Prophet couldn't sleep that night, hearing him groan in his ropes, until they were loosened.
screen: `THEY GAVE THE ENEMY THE BREAD.` · `FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, NO THANKS.` · `TEACH TEN CHILDREN TO WRITE.` · `ZAYD, THE FUTURE SCRIBE.` · then, large: `FREEDOM FOR TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach someone something. Sit, and think of one thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't. How to cook a dish. How to change a tire. A phrase in another language. A shortcut on the computer. How to make wudu, if that's yours to teach. Picture the person, and the moment you'd show them, patiently, the way the prisoners of Badr taught children to shape their letters. The bell holds the time.
Mercy to captives. After Badr, prisoners were fed with the better food, and some were freed for teaching Muslim children to read and write. Today's word.
Your line: freedom for teaching. Today, teach that one small thing to someone, and let them keep it. Day two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite the captives of Badr and Qur'an 76:8 when teaching about the humane treatment of prisoners, and the ransom of literacy is remembered as an early honoring of learning.

fork.reveal: teach ten children to read and write, and go free. a community fighting to survive asked its enemies for literacy.

original.note: Arabic: a captive, a prisoner. the word used in 76:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: captives in old wars were treated badly.
what it means: after Badr, prisoners were fed the better food, and some were freed for teaching children to write.
what a scholar hears: the literacy ransom rests on a report of Ibn 'Abbas in Musnad Ahmad and on Ibn Sa'd; Zayd ibn Thabit's name is linked to it in the Tabaqat.

sources.ref: Qur'an 76:8–9 (feeding the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, for the love of God)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): Abu 'Aziz ibn 'Umayr on the bread and dates
Musnad Ahmad 2216 (teaching ten children as ransom, from Ibn 'Abbas)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: the literacy ransom; Zayd ibn Thabit; al-'Abbas's ropes

notes: Musnad Ahmad number and the Zayd ibn Thabit link cited from memory; the Zayd detail is 'tradition says'. Confirm.
76:8 is often dated to Medina and linked by some commentators to other occasions; the script says 'a later surah' only. Confirm.
Left out: the debate over ransom versus execution and 8:67–69, and the two captives reported executed on the way back. A Keeper may want that told honestly somewhere; flagged.
Al-'Abbas's ropes loosened: from Ibn Sa'd; confirm.
